It serves as backup detail for agenda item 8.A. at the August 16, 2022 regular meeting.

Scopes of work by building:
- Troy High School: replacement of all cameras; video intercom at the main entrance; adding a video intercom station for food-service deliveries; two viewing/intercom stations included.
- Athens High School: same scope as Troy High - replacement of all cameras; main-entrance video intercom; food-service delivery intercom station; two viewing/intercom stations.
- Central Office/Administration building: adding a video intercom station at the main entrance; cameras on the building exterior and on the interior at the main entrance; two viewing/intercom stations.
- Services building: adding a video intercom station at the main entrance; cameras on the building exterior; two viewing/intercom stations.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A recommendation letter dated August 10, 2022, on letterhead of Convergent Technology Partners (6197 Miller Road, Ste #4, Swartz Creek, MI 48473; phone 810.720.3820; e-mail info@ctpartners.net; website www.ctpartners.net), addressed to Beth Soggs, Technology Director, Troy School District. Subject: "Security Upgrades RFP #9948 Recommendation Letter." It supports agenda item 8.A. at the August 16, 2022 regular Board of Education meeting.

Solicitation process: On July 5, 2022, the Troy School District issued a Request for Proposal (RFP) soliciting bids for district-wide security upgrades. The RFP was posted to the District's and the State's websites, and Convergent spoke with several vendors and directed them to the websites to download the RFP and supporting documentation to ensure a good bidding pool. On July 26, 2022, sealed bids were accepted and opened by the district; five proposals were received.

Initial results were tabulated as: AmComm $304,540.00; Moss Audio Corporation $420,300.73; AOB dba Security Designs $548,916.00; Securatech $634,688.39; Master Electric $640,542.87.

All proposals were evaluated for compliance with the RFP requirements, pricing, technical solution, and acceptance of the RFP's terms and conditions. Findings:
- AmComm was determined to be non-compliant, as not all portions of the RFP were bid and the video intercom and most camera-type quantities for what was bid were incorrect.
- Moss Audio was determined to be non-compliant due to the quantity of missing cameras.
- Security Designs was determined to be compliant.
- Securatech did not include the cost for the PLM bond of $31,734.41 on the bid form, which, once included, put them as the high bidder; otherwise they appear compliant.
- Master Electric was determined to be compliant.

Revised compliant bid tabulation: AOB dba Security Designs $548,916.00; Master Electric $640,542.87; Securatech $666,422.80.

Recommendation: Security Designs had a satisfactory interview by the District and Convergent Technology Partners, and Convergent has worked with the company in the past with favorable results. Based on these factors, Convergent recommends the award of the Security Upgrades (RFP #9948) project to the low qualified bidder, Security Designs, in the amount of $548,916.00, with an additional approximately 5% contingency of $27,445.00, for a total of $576,361.00.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A Board of Education workshop presentation delivered September 6, 2022, titled 'Summer Professional Learning and Summer School Update,' summarizing how Troy School District used the summer of 2022 for staff development and expanded student learning.

Staff professional learning. Under a 'OneTroy Summer Learning' banner, offerings included Technology Integration: Digital Media, Summer Curriculum Development, an Administrative Kick-Off Meeting, a Teaching and Learning Team Retreat, a Cabinet Retreat, Board Learning with education author Tony Wagner, the TSD Literacy Project, Pre-K Literacy, Troy Institutes K-12, a High School Writing Institute, New Teacher Orientation, and a Math Recovery Institute. Principal retreats and the admin kick-off focused on reviewing the district's Mission, Vision, Values, and thematic goals, on bond engagement and communication materials, and on ALICE trainer training so administrators can lead safety training across all TSD facilities. The TSD Literacy Project reached over 100 teachers across grade bands K-2, 3-5, 6-8, and 9-10, with specific phonics work for K-2 and continued use of the Workshop Method PreK-10. The Preschool Literacy Institute drew over 30 staff in its sixth year, and New Teacher Orientation ran four days.

Student summer programming. A program-summary table lists enrollment and location: K-7 Multilingual 130 (Morse/Troy Union); K-5 Multilingual Immersion 75; 8-12 Multilingual 15; K-5 Title I (50 in-person, 15+ virtual, at Morse); K-6 Littera tutoring 400 (virtual/contracted); K-8 Math Champs / Math Recovery 1:1 110 (virtual/contracted); 3-5 Math Classroom 240 (virtual); AYD Grade K-5 Math 100+ (virtual); Reading Recovery 1:1 16 (in person); Math Recovery 25 (virtual); Extended School Year (ESY) 200 (in person); all-elementary building support about 30 per building; Troy Union Title I 40+; and Morse Summer Nights 150. A featured program, Littera Tutoring and Math Recovery, ran virtual 30-minute sessions three to four times weekly for seven weeks and, combined with the spring session, served over 400 K-6 students, with spring-to-fall growth comparisons pending the assessment window.

Community outreach included Troy Union Summer Literacy Meet-Ups -- four park events across the summer (approximately 50 families on July 7, 30 on July 20, and over 250 people at the August 17 end-of-summer celebration) featuring a traveling library, plus a Padlet to keep families connected.

Community Education summer school reported in-seat PE-only enrollment of 123 students (Session 1) and 118 (Session 2); virtual Edgenuity enrollment of 1,002 students across 1,568 classes, with 75% of enrollment in grades 8-10; a Math Honors Academy (Bridge and Math 8) of 27 students; and COVID credit recovery for grades 9-12 with 611 courses taken and 399 credits earned.

Finally, the Troy Summer Learning Lab -- a free program for students entering grades 6-8 -- used the Stanford design-thinking process, opening with two weeks of immersion featuring guest speakers and field trips before students defined problems, ideated, and prototyped solutions; it enrolled 129 students from all four district middle schools and engaged 21 TSD staff. The presentation is an informational update emphasizing reach, flexible delivery models, grant funding, and positive parent and staff feedback.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A proposal for Education Design Services from Fielding International -- a school-design firm at 460 Hilton Road, Ferndale, Michigan 48220 (fieldingintl.com), with offices in Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Rhode Island, and Singapore -- submitted to Troy School District as agenda item 3.B. The cover letter is dated July 15, 2022 and is addressed to Ms. Christine DiPalato, Assistant Superintendent, Troy School District, 440 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098; an internal proposal section is dated June 20, 2022.

Purpose and framing. Fielding proposes to support the district 'as it explores a new vision for what middle school teaching and learning might look like now and in the future.' The scope would facilitate an engagement and planning process to form a vision representing a shift in teaching-and-learning priorities that better aligns with strong interdisciplinary programming while supporting student wellness and social-emotional learning. The work would begin by auditing staff and student perceptions of the school experience, use those insights to design a new 'learning ecosystem' concept (including physical-space concepts), and then transition into a process-consulting phase in which Fielding's educators and designers work alongside district leadership and key staff on detailed planning, implementation, and sustaining success. The letter frames this as an opportunity to align a school's vision, programmatic priorities, and physical environment.

Phase 1 - Pre-Discovery and Framing. This phase gathers contextual information about the current state of Troy's middle-school programs and aspirations for a re-imagined future, beginning with meetings and data collection. The Fielding team would host one-on-one, 30-minute virtual meetings with a selection of school leaders to hear individual aspirations; ideal interviewees are the building leaders at Troy's four middle schools plus district leaders engaged in the process.

Phase 2 - Program and Environment Discovery. The central component is a multi-day immersive site visit during which the Fielding team completes structured observations of the middle-school experience and conducts informal interviews with students, teachers, and staff to capture quantitative and qualitative data on how teaching and learning are delivered and to identify misalignments between district and school leaders' aspirations, the physical learning environments, and the actual student experience. The team would debrief immediate findings at the end of the visit. Fielding would also introduce school models demonstrating future-ready physical designs and programmatic approaches to middle-years learning, and an optional and 'highly recommended' visit by Troy staff to another innovative school is offered. The phase's deliverable is a 'Teaching, Learning, and Future Facilities Discovery Report' synthesizing the discovery findings, highlighting core pillars of the district's future, identifying misalignments between current practice and aspirations, and prioritizing areas of growth.

This document is a recommendation memorandum from the district's policy counsel outlining proposed updates to several Troy School District board policies, presented at the September 20, 2022 regular meeting of the Board of Education. It is organized by policy series: Bylaws (1000 Series), Students (2000 Series), and Curriculum and Instruction (3000 Series).

Under the Bylaws, Policy 1000.01 (Organization and Functioning of the Board: Removal from Office) is addressed. Because the policy is intended to address the removal of board officers from their officer positions, not removal of the Board itself, counsel recommends changing the sub-policy heading to "Removal from Officer Positions" to eliminate ambiguity.

Under Students, Policy 2000.01 (Admission and Enrollment: Children of Non-Resident Employees) is updated consistent with language in the State Aid Act and the Pupil Accounting Manual. The change follows discovery of a loophole in which a person could obtain employment, enroll their child under the sub-policy, then voluntarily leave employment while the pupil maintained enrollment without paying tuition. The recommended language provides that a child of a non-resident employee may enroll without tuition if enrolling in the K-12 program; once enrolled, the student may continue to attend through graduation or receipt of a certificate of completion as long as the employee remains employed; and the student may also continue if the employee no longer works for the district due to layoff or elimination of the position. It preserves the district's ability to impose long-term suspension or expulsion for Student Code of Conduct violations, defines "employee" as an individual with regularly scheduled hours while school is in session (excluding seasonal, coaching, or third-party contracted employees, including substitute teachers), and makes the benefit effective at the start of the next school term/semester.

Policy 2000.06 (Behavior: Personal Electronic Devices) adds language making clear that students may not use cell phones or similar devices to record or take pictures of other individuals at school without permission, subject to common-sense exceptions such as recording a sporting event or arts performance meant to be publicly viewed. The revised sub-policy reserves the district's right to prohibit possession or use of personal electronic devices on district property or at district-related functions; permits student use only before and after the regular school day, during the student's scheduled lunch, or as directed by staff for educational purposes; requires devices otherwise to be powered off and kept out of sight in backpacks, purses, or lockers; and prohibits broadcasting or recording audio, images, or video of any student, staff member, or other person without permission, except for curricular or extra-curricular activities where recording is generally permitted (e.g., athletic events, arts performances). The Superintendent may develop regulations to further control possession and use.

Policy 2000.07 (Health and Safety: Wellness) is revised at both the policy level and the administrative-regulation level (2000.07-AR) to bring the district into compliance with the latest regulatory guidance and interpretations, given increased federal attention to student wellness and nutrition. The updated language recognizes that student wellness is integral to learning, growth, and development, commits the district to promoting proper nutrition, nutrition education, and regular physical activity, and confirms the Board has adopted a periodically reviewed Wellness Policy, with the Superintendent to develop implementing regulations.

The document then turns to the Curriculum and Instruction (3000 Series), noting that, given the current political environment and escalating attacks on schools and boards relative to curriculum development and approval, counsel spent considerable time carefully reviewing and revising the entire series; the extracted text is truncated at this point.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Agenda item 2.E. from the Troy School District Board of Education meeting of September 20, 2022, is a suggested resolution recognizing September 2022 as National Suicide Prevention Month. The item explains that Oakland Community Health Network (OCHN) asked school boards throughout Oakland County to partner with them by approving such a proclamation at their September board meetings. The recommended action is acceptance of the resolution, which includes "Moved by" and "Supported by" lines and YES/NO vote tallies.

The resolution's WHEREAS clauses set out its rationale and supporting statistics: September is known as National Suicide Prevention Month, intended to raise awareness of prevention resources available in the community; World Suicide Prevention Day is observed each year on September 10; and suicidal thoughts can affect anyone regardless of age, gender, race, orientation, income level, religion, or background. Citing the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the resolution states that 45,979 people died by suicide in the United States in 2020 - one death every 11 minutes - and that 12.2 million adults across the U.S. seriously thought about suicide, 3.2 million made a suicide plan, and 1.2 million attempted suicide. Citing the 2020 Michigan Suicide Prevention Commission Annual Report, it notes that 1,389 people in the state died by suicide during the COVID-19 pandemic, with 1,099 of those deaths relating to men.

Further clauses observe that thousands of individuals die by suicide each year, leaving behind friends and family to navigate the tragedy of loss, and that feelings of shame and stigma often prevent open discussion. The resolution notes that 988 has been designated as the new three-digit dialing code that routes callers to the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline and is now active across the United States, and that the National Action Alliance for Suicide Prevention uses #BeThere to educate social media followers about the many actions one can take to support a person who is struggling. It further recognizes that OCHN has been an active and engaged member of the Oakland County Suicide Prevention Task Force since 2011 and is committed to being a Zero Suicide organization, cultivating a network of providers who are engaged in the Zero Suicide philosophy.

The resolving clause states: NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Oakland Community Health Network hereby recognizes September 2022 as National Suicide Prevention Month, and that OCHN calls upon citizens, government agencies, public and private institutions, businesses, and schools to recommit the state to increasing awareness and understanding of suicide prevention and the need for appropriate and accessible services to assist individuals in crisis.

A memorandum dated August 31, 2022 from Rick West, Assistant Superintendent of Business Services, to the Troy School District Board of Education, with copies to Rich Machesky and Christine DiPilato, concerning the selection of professional service providers for the district's bond program. The memo explains that TMP Architecture and Barton Malow had already been engaged throughout the district's pre-bond work and would continue through the election, and that the district remains satisfied with both partnerships and the institutional knowledge the firms bring to the design and build process. In June 2022 the district asked each firm to submit a proposal to continue its services throughout the bond program. Dr. Machesky, Christine DiPilato, Michelle Kerns, and Rick West reviewed the proposals, interviewed the firms, and recommend that the Board approve a resolution in September authorizing staff to negotiate final contract terms with both firms based on their submitted proposals. West expresses confidence that negotiation will produce market-competitive agreements providing quality services.

The memo further recommends continuing the services of Lecole Planners, represented by Michelle Kerns, as the district's Owner's Representative for construction projects, describing Lecole as a strong partner that works with TMP, Barton Malow, and other contractors to keep projects on time and within budget; these services would be included in the resolution. Finally, the memo recommends engaging Fielding International to provide a scope of work aimed at aligning designs with the district's strategic plan and taking a deep dive into instructional practice and delivery, specifically at the middle level. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A workshop presentation reviewing Troy School District graduation requirements and their impact on alternative education. The Michigan Department of Education requires 18 specified credits; TSD requires 4.5 additional credits (0.5 PE and 4.0 electives), for 22.5 total, while students at Troy High and Athens High can earn 6.0 credits per year. The study examines credit recovery, the TCCHS alternative program, peer-district comparisons, and whether to offer a distinct "Troy School District" diploma for students completing alternative programs.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
Board workshop presentation, "Graduation Requirements," for Troy School District.

Goals
- Review TSD graduation requirements.
- Discuss impact on alternative education.
- Review peer district graduation requirements.
- Decide next steps for alternative ed and future study for comprehensive schools.

TSD requirements
- MDE requires 18 specified credits.
- TSD requires 4.5 additional credits: 0.5 PE and 4.0 elective credits (22.5 total).
- Students at Troy High School and Athens High School can earn 6.0 credits each year in a traditional academic year.

Alternative education (TCCHS)
- Credit recovery lets students make up lost credits and move more quickly through curriculum.
- TCCHS features a smaller learning environment, wrap-around support, 4 classes per quarter, Wednesday support, and 8 credits per year.

Considerations
- Whether to offer a "Troy School District" diploma for students completing alternative programs, while keeping school-specific diplomas (AHS/THS diploma at 22.5 credits).
- What TCCHS graduates should accomplish before earning a diploma; other concerns about alternative learning pathways.

Peer comparison
- Many peer Michigan districts require only 0.5 Health and 0.5 PE (without TSD's extra 0.5).
- TSD's total credit requirement is at the higher end but competitive; peers were selected based on typical student academic performance.

Purpose
Informs board discussion on whether to further study graduation requirements for AHS, THS, and alternative programs.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This presentation, titled "Graduation Requirements" and marked District/School Troy, was prepared for a Board of Education workshop to review the district's graduation requirements and their implications for alternative education. Its stated goals are to review TSD graduation requirements, discuss the impact on alternative education, review peer district graduation requirements, and decide on next steps for alternative education and future study for the comprehensive high schools.

On requirements, the presentation states that the Michigan Department of Education (MDE) requirements include 18 specified credits, and that TSD requires 4.5 additional credits consisting of 0.5 PE and 4.0 elective credits, for a total of 22.5. It notes that students at Troy High School (THS) and Athens High School (AHS) can earn 6.0 credits each year in a traditional academic year.

A section on credit recovery describes it as an opportunity to make up credits lost and to move more quickly through the curriculum. Regarding TCCHS, the presentation lists its focus on meeting student needs through student support, a smaller learning environment, and wrap-around support, with a learning structure of 4 classes per quarter, Wednesday support, and 8 credits per year.

Under considerations, the slides pose questions about what is most important for TCCHS graduates to accomplish before earning a high school diploma and whether the district might offer a "Troy School District" diploma for students who complete alternative programs, while maintaining the opportunity to earn school-specific diplomas aligned to program requirements (for example, an AHS/THS diploma for 22.5 credits). They also ask what other concerns arise when thinking about alternative learning pathways.

A peer district comparison section states that many peer Michigan districts only require 0.5 Health and 0.5 PE credits (without TSD's additional 0.5), that the total credit requirement based on credits possible is at the higher end but competitive, and that peer districts were selected based on typical student academic performance.

The presentation closes with additional considerations, asking whether the board has interest in further studying the graduation requirements for AHS and THS, and what additional information would be helpful in preparing for a review of comprehensive graduation requirements, followed by a questions slide. Several slides in the source appear to be image or chart placeholders without extracted text. Overall, the document frames a policy discussion rather than presenting a decision, inviting the board to direct next steps for both alternative and comprehensive graduation requirements.

Dated September 15, 2022, this memorandum from Rick West to the Troy Board of Education outlines recommended updates to the District's Policy Manual and provides the rationale for each contemplated change. The revisions were recommended jointly by Miller Johnson School Policy Services, the Board of Education Policy Committee, and District Administration, and are organized by Policy Manual section (Introduction 0000 series, Bylaws 1000 series, and Students 2000 series). The file is associated with the October 4, 2022 board workshop.

Policy 0000.03, The Superintendent of Schools, would receive two additions. The first confirms that the Superintendent, as the district's chief administrator employed under the Revised School Code, is authorized to make employment decisions -- including hiring and termination -- for all non-administrative and non-teaching staff, and is responsible for developing Administrative Regulations (which generally take effect one month after being provided to the Board unless otherwise agreed, and which the Board may but need not formally approve). The second specifies that the Board is represented in labor negotiations by a negotiating team whose members the Board approves before negotiations begin; the Superintendent selects the bargaining team, and all negotiated agreements are subject to Board ratification.

Policy 1000.01, Organization and Functioning of the Board, would rename its 'Removal from Office' sub-policy to 'Removal from Officer Positions'. The change clarifies that the provision governs removing board officers from their officer positions, not removal from the Board itself.

Policy 2000.01, Admission and Enrollment, would revise the 'Children of Non-Resident Employees' sub-policy to close a loophole in which a person could gain employment, enroll a child tuition-free, then voluntarily leave employment while the child remained enrolled without paying tuition. The recommended language allows a child of a non-resident employee to enroll without tuition if enrolling in the K-12 program and to continue through graduation while the employee remains employed -- and also to continue attending if the employee no longer works for the district due to layoff or elimination of the position (while not barring long-term suspension or expulsion for Student Code of Conduct violations). It defines an employee as an individual with regularly scheduled hours while school is in session, excluding seasonal, coaching, or third-party contracted employees (including substitute teachers), with eligibility beginning at the start of the next school term or semester.

Policy 2000.06, Behavior: Personal Electronic Devices, would add language -- under the 'Distribution and Posting of Materials' sub-policy -- making clear that students may not use cell phones or similar devices to record or photograph other individuals at school without permission, subject to common-sense exceptions such as recording a sporting event, arts performance, or other activity meant to be publicly viewed. The memo was issued by the district Business Office at 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098 (phone 248.823.4022, fax 248.823.4013).

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A policy-manual update memo from MJ School Policy Services to MJ Policy Service Clients, dated September 19, 2022, concerning Policy 1002, "Meetings of the Board of Education," and specifically remote participation by board members under Michigan's Open Meetings Act (OMA). The memo recaps that the firm's July 2022 update had included, under the "Meeting Procedures" subheading, an "Electronic Meetings and Remote Participation" section stating that remote participation should be limited, that remote participants may not constitute a quorum, and that remote participation was allowed only when necessitated by military duty, a medical condition, or a local state of emergency/disaster. That language is now expressly labeled "outdated as of 9/16/22 update." The earlier language also set conditions for remote attendance: the Board Secretary must name each remotely attending member in the minutes; the remote member must hear and be heard; the member must notify the Board President at least one business day before the meeting; and the Board President must ensure the public is aware of how any remote member voted, such as by roll-call voting.

The memo states that this language generated significant internal discussion within the MJ Education Law Team and client requests for clarification about the permissible level of remote board participation. In response, the firm presents two options for clients. Both options now permit remote participation only on the basis of (1) absence due to military leave or (2) a reasonable accommodation required because of a disability. Language pertaining to a medical condition or local state of emergency/disaster has been removed because the OMA no longer permits remote participation on those bases; under the OMA, only a board member absent due to military duty may (and, in fact, must) be permitted to attend remotely.

The memo cites an opinion letter released earlier that year by Attorney General Nessel, which provides that a board member with a disability must be accommodated, so that if the only reasonable accommodation available is remote participation, the member is entitled to it. A footnote explains that although the OMA contains no such exception, the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) negates the OMA to the extent that following the OMA would require violating the ADA. The firm acknowledges client concern that a strict reading of the COVID-19-era OMA amendments would let a non-military, non-disabled member only listen remotely but not voice an opinion or vote on a pending matter. Noting that prior Attorney General opinions had generally allowed remote participation so long as the remote member was not used to establish a quorum or cast the deciding vote, the firm takes the position that board members may still contribute to meetings remotely, even without a military-duty absence or disability accommodation, provided they are not used to constitute a quorum and are not permitted to be the deciding vote on a motion. It adds that if a member is participating remotely because of military duty or a disability accommodation, other board members may not also contribute remotely.
